panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Frontal abdominal radiograph of a 5-year-old boy explicitly stated to have MMIHS, showing marked dilation of multiple bowel loops, a captioned manifestation matching the MMIHS vocabulary finding of dilated bowel loops/ileus pattern; the article is a disease-focused pictorial review of MMIHS imaging. b: Contrast study through the ileostomy in the same 5-year-old boy with MMIHS showing dilated bowel loops (MMIHS vocabulary finding) plus a narrowed channel at the ostomy (arrow), which is a post-surgical complication rather than a primary disease manifestation, hence lower confidence and variant typicality. c: Sagittal CT with enteric contrast in the same 5-year-old boy with MMIHS demonstrating severe upstream dilation of bowel loops (a captioned MMIHS-associated manifestation) with an arrow marking ostomy narrowing, a post-surgical complication; disease attribution rests on the explicit MMIHS diagnosis plus the captioned bowel dilatation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Four-frame upper GI study with small bowel follow-through in an infant with MMIHS (Fam28-1) due to de novo ACTG2 mutation; arrows mark contrast position at 0 h, 2 h, 6 h and 2 days demonstrating markedly delayed transit and retrograde reflux into the stomach without obstructive lesion, i.e. hypoperistalsis. Caption and article title directly attribute the patient to MMIHS. B: Two axial abdominal CT slices from an adolescent MMIHS patient (Fam26-1) showing multiple distended bowel loops with air-fluid levels marked by arrows, a recognized manifestation of the hypoperistalsis/intestinal dysmotility of MMIHS. C: Voiding cystourethrogram in an infant male with MMIHS (Fam29-1) demonstrating a grossly distended (megacystis) contrast-filled bladder, one of the defining features of megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome.

panels.figure_caption: Radiologic features of MMIHS due to de novo ACTG2 mutations. A.) An infant subject from our cohort (Fam28-1) underwent an upper GI study with small bowel follow-through. Contrast was administered beyond the pylorus (left panel, arrow) in this patient who had undergone a previous Ladd procedure. At two hours, the contrast has mostly passed retrograde back into the stomach (arrow) contrary to expectations. At six hours, the contrast is in the small intestine (arrow) and has not reached the colon. At two days, contrast material is still present in the colon (arrow) suggesting a severely delayed transit of material in the GI tract consistent with hypoperistalsis. No physical obstructive lesions are visualized. B.) An abdominal CT scan on an adolescent patient with MMIHS (Fam26-1). The patient has a diverting ileostomy, but multiple distended bowel loops with air-fluid levels (arrows) are seen at the level of the sacrum (left) and lumbar spine (right). C.) A voiding cystourethrogram on an infant male subject (Fam29-1) showing a grossly distended bladder.
